set1.q: A 76-year-old man has spells of palpitations and near-fainting. A 24-hour monitor shows runs of a fast rhythm that alternate with slow beats and long pauses (tachy-brady syndrome). Which rhythm most often produces the fast runs?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast phase, and then the pacemaker needs a defibrillator, but the most common tachyarrhythmia in tachy-brady syndrome is atrial fibrillation.
Atrial flutter is a regular sawtooth rhythm common after atrial scarring; it is not the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome, which is most often atrial fibrillation.
Sinus tachycardia is a physiologic or pathologic response with a P wave before each beat; the fast runs of tachy-brady syndrome are most often atrial fibrillation.
Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome a tachyarrhythmia alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or pauses, and the most common tachyarrhythmia is atrial fibrillation.

set1.q: A 63-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy is told that his episode of palpitations was sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which description best fits that rhythm?
opts: Chaotic waves with no true QRS complexes
Chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no QRS complexes is ventricular fibrillation, with no pulse; ventricular tachycardia has organized wide complexes.
Regular, wide QRS complexes of one shape

Correct. Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is regular at 100 to 250 with wide QRS complexes over 0.12 seconds that all share the same shape and no P waves tied to them; sustained means 30 seconds or more.

Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is regular at 100 to 250 with every QRS the same shape, so an irregular rhythm near 300 does not fit; a wide rhythm whose QRS shape varies is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.
Regular, narrow QRS with hidden P waves
A regular narrow tachycardia with hidden P waves is supraventricular, such as nodal reentry; ventricular tachycardia has a wide QRS over 0.12 seconds.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with pneumonia and severe hypoxia becomes unresponsive. No pulse can be felt, yet the monitor shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 80 with a P wave before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no QRS complexes; this monitor shows regular, narrow complexes with P waves.
ruled out by a stated finding
The tracing looks like normal sinus rhythm, but there is no pulse and no perfusion, which makes it pulseless electrical activity, a cardiac arrest.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. An organized rhythm you would expect to produce a pulse, with no perfusing beats, is pulseless electrical activity, not asystole; hypoxia and hypovolemia are its two leading causes in adults.
Asystole is a flat line with no P waves and no QRS complexes; this monitor shows an organized rhythm, which without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with chest pain develops a wide tachycardia whose QRS shape varies from beat to beat; his QT interval was normal earlier. He is defibrillated and returns to sinus rhythm. Which study is the most urgent next?
opts: Ambulatory monitoring confirms whether symptoms match intermittent bradycardia; an ischemic polymorphic tachycardia needs urgent coronary angiography.
Digoxin toxicity is a listed cause of junctional rhythm and of block; polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with chest pain and a normal QT points to ischemia.
The stroke-risk score guides anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation; after polymorphic ventricular tachycardia from ischemia the priority is coronary angiography.
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia without a long QT is most often from acute ischemia, so after defibrillation it needs urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization.

set1.q: A 20-year-old man with a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 220 converts to sinus rhythm with adenosine. An accessory pathway is suspected. Which tracing is most useful for looking for it?
opts: Coronary angiography looks for ischemia after polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; an accessory pathway is an electrical finding seen on a sinus-rhythm tracing.

Correct. Pre-excitation (a short PR interval and a slurred QRS upstroke, the delta wave) shows on a tracing in sinus rhythm and is consistent with an accessory pathway; a narrow, orthodromic tachycardia shows no delta wave.
During a narrow, orthodromic reentrant tachycardia the impulse goes down the atrioventricular node, so the QRS is normal with no delta wave; the pathway shows in sinus rhythm.
Electrolytes matter for premature ventricular contractions and long QT; an accessory pathway is found by its short PR and delta wave on a sinus tracing.

set1.q: A 55-year-old man has a preoperative electrocardiogram and no symptoms. The rhythm is sinus at 72, the QRS lasts 0.16 seconds, V1 to V3 show an rsR' pattern (a second upward deflection, bunny ears), and there is a slurred S wave in I and aVL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds with an rsR' pattern (bunny ears) in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL is right bundle branch block; it is usually asymptomatic and is not always pathologic when new.
Left bundle branch block widens the QRS with a dominant S wave (rS) in V1 and monophasic R waves in the lateral leads; an rsR' in V1 to V3 is right-sided.
Wolff-Parkinson-White shows a short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave); a second upward deflection in V1 to V3 is a right bundle branch block.
Ventricular tachycardia is a wide rhythm at 100 to 250 with no P waves tied to the QRS; he is in sinus rhythm at 72.

set1.q: A 24-year-old man collapses during a basketball game and wakes within a minute. In the ambulance his rhythm is irregular, with wide QRS complexes of varying width at rates approaching 300. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial flutter with 2:1 block is regular with narrow QRS complexes and sawtooth waves; this rhythm is irregular and wide.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular but narrow, with three or more P-wave shapes, in acutely ill lung patients; this rhythm is wide and near 300.

Correct. An irregular, wide-complex rhythm with rates approaching 300 is atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway (with Wolff-Parkinson-White); ventricular tachycardia is regular at 150 to 200.
Ventricular tachycardia is the other wide-complex tachycardia, but it is regular at about 150 to 200; this rhythm is irregular and approaches 300.

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has a preoperative 12-lead electrocardiogram, which is shown. The QRS lasts 0.16 seconds. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Wolff-Parkinson-White shows a short PR and a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave); this pattern of deep V1 complexes and broad lateral R waves is a bundle branch block.

Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds with a deep, dominant S wave in V1 and broad, upright lateral complexes without Q waves in I, V5 and V6 is left bundle branch block; chronic hypertension is a common cause.
Right bundle branch block gives an rsR' pattern (a second upward deflection) in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL; here V1 to V3 are deep and downward.
Ventricular tachycardia is a regular wide rhythm at 100 to 250; this tracing has wide complexes at a normal rate, from slowed conduction in one bundle.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man reports frequent skipped beats. His electrocardiogram shows many early beats, each with an abnormally shaped P wave and a narrow QRS. Which is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
opts: No treatment or workup is needed for infrequent premature atrial contractions without symptoms; frequent ones warrant a look for structural heart disease.
Correct. Early beats with abnormal P waves and narrow QRS complexes are premature atrial contractions; when they are frequent, the next step is to look for underlying structural heart disease.
Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation and flutter; premature atrial contractions are a benign rhythm, and frequent ones call for a structural workup.
Urgent angiography follows defibrillation of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; frequent premature atrial contractions call for a search for structural heart disease.

set1.q: A 74-year-old woman has episodes of lightheadedness. Her office electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 64, but her family has noticed a slow pulse during the spells. Which is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is for symptomatic bradycardia once symptoms are shown to correlate with it; that correlation has not yet been confirmed.
Urgent coronary angiography follows defibrillation of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia from ischemia; intermittent slow spells need ambulatory monitoring first.
Observation is appropriate only if symptoms turn out not to match bradycardia; that has to be established by monitoring before she is reassured.

Correct. In suspected sick sinus syndrome the key step is to confirm whether symptoms correlate with episodes of bradycardia, as a 24-hour ambulatory recording does; with correlation a pacemaker follows, without it observation is appropriate.

set1.q: A 28-year-old woman has had a pounding heartbeat for 30 minutes that began suddenly. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 118/76. The monitor reads a regular rate of 170, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Adenosine is the right drug for stable supraventricular tachycardia, but it comes second: the first-line step in a stable patient is a vagal maneuver.
Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia; she is alert with a normal blood pressure.
Procainamide is used for atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway, an irregular wide rhythm; this strip is regular and narrow, so a vagal maneuver comes first.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves is supraventricular tachycardia (here typical nodal reentry); in a stable patient a vagal maneuver comes first, then adenosine if it fails.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with hypertension has had palpitations for a week. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 132/80, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the first goal of treatment?
opts: Correct. Narrow complexes at irregularly irregular intervals with no P waves are atrial fibrillation; in a hemodynamically stable patient the first goal is rate control, with anticoagulation decided by the stroke-risk score.
Synchronized cardioversion now is for hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation; she is alert and normotensive, so rate control comes first.
Adenosine treats regular supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver; this rhythm is irregularly irregular with no P waves, and the goal is rate control.
Mapping and ablation are a later option in atrial fibrillation; the first goal in a stable patient is rate control, then anticoagulation.
set1.alt: Rhythm strip of narrow complexes at visibly unequal intervals over a wavy baseline with no clear P waves

set1.q: A 48-year-old woman started a medication known to prolong the QT interval last week. She now has palpitations but is awake and talking, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Adenosine treats regular narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia; this is a wide, polymorphic ventricular rhythm that needs magnesium.

Correct. A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose complexes twist around the baseline in a patient with a long QT is torsades de pointes; in a conscious patient intravenous magnesium breaks it, then more magnesium as an infusion.
Amiodarone (like procainamide) is avoided in torsades de pointes because it prolongs the QT further; magnesium is the treatment.
Beta blockers are avoided in torsades de pointes: the bradycardia they cause lengthens the R-to-R interval and indirectly the QT.
set1.alt: Rhythm strip of a rapid, wide-complex rhythm whose complexes grow taller, shrink, then grow again, as if turning around the baseline

set1.q: A 40-year-old man has a stable, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 180. It is unclear whether the rhythm comes from a focus in the atria or a reentry circuit that uses the atrioventricular node. Which agent is most useful as a diagnostic tool?
opts: Correct. Adenosine is an important diagnostic tool here: it usually terminates reentry that depends on the atrioventricular node but is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia, so the response separates them.
Amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, but it does not separate an atrial focus from a node-dependent circuit; adenosine does.
Procainamide is used for atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway; adenosine, not procainamide, is the diagnostic tool for a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
Magnesium treats torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular rhythm with a long QT; it has no diagnostic role in a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.

set1.q: A 35-year-old woman has abrupt-onset palpitations. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 170, with one P wave of the same abnormal shape before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia has a uniform, normal P wave and runs from 100 to 160; her P waves are abnormal in shape and the rate is 170.
ruled out by a stated finding
Nodal reentrant tachycardia hides its P waves, a reentry circuit within the atrioventricular node; she has a visible abnormal P wave before every QRS.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with one consistently abnormal P wave before each QRS comes from a single ectopic focus in the atria outside the sinus node: focal atrial tachycardia, which typically begins abruptly.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three different P-wave shapes in the same lead; her rhythm is regular with one P-wave shape.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman has had stable atrial fibrillation for 2 months. Her rate is now controlled, but she would like her normal rhythm restored. Which must come before an outpatient cardioversion?
opts: Correct. In stable atrial fibrillation the first goal is rate control and the second anticoagulation; outpatient cardioversion is done after 21 days of anticoagulation.
Adenosine treats or unmasks regular supraventricular tachycardia; it has no place before cardioversion of atrial fibrillation, which needs 21 days of anticoagulation.
A pacemaker treats symptomatic bradycardia and high-grade block; restoring sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation needs 21 days of anticoagulation first.
Rate control is the first goal in atrial fibrillation and continues; what must precede outpatient cardioversion is 21 days of anticoagulation.

set1.q: A 30-year-old marathon runner has no symptoms. A lead II tracing taken at rest is shown; the rate is 48. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular; these complexes are evenly spaced, slow and regular, with no fibrillating baseline.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 40 to 60 with no P waves visible (hidden in the QRS) is a junctional rhythm, which can be seen in healthy, well-conditioned athletes with increased vagal tone.
Sinus bradycardia, also common in athletes, has an upright P wave before every QRS; this tracing shows no P wave before any of the complexes.
ruled out by a stated finding
Third-degree block shows P waves marching at their own rate, unrelated to a slow escape rhythm; this tracing has no P waves to march.
set1.alt: Lead II rhythm strip of five narrow complexes at a slow, regular rate, each followed by a T wave, with no P wave visible before any complex

set1.q: A 70-year-old man with prior cardiac surgery has a regular rhythm at 150 with sawtooth atrial waves, two for every narrow QRS. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 128/78. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial flutter; he is alert with a normal blood pressure, so rate control comes first.
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway; stable atrial flutter is treated with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
A permanent pacemaker treats symptomatic bradycardia and high-grade block; a fast, stable atrial flutter needs rate control and later ablation.

Correct. Sawtooth waves conducted 2:1 make atrial flutter; when hemodynamically stable it is treated with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker for rate control, though control is harder to reach than in atrial fibrillation.

set1.q: A 67-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has palpitations and dyspnea. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 150, with two sawtooth atrial waves before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia has one upright P wave before each QRS; she has two identical sawtooth waves for every QRS.
Focal atrial tachycardia has one abnormal P wave per QRS from a single focus; two sawtooth waves per QRS is the 2:1 block of atrial flutter.

Correct. Sawtooth atrial waves outnumbering the QRS complexes, here two to one (the most common block), make atrial flutter, which is common with pulmonary vascular disease or right-sided heart failure.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no organized atrial waves; her rhythm is regular with repeating sawtooth waves.

set1.q: A 17-year-old soccer player had an episode of racing heartbeat that stopped on its own. His resting tracing, taken in sinus rhythm, is shown. Which description best fits this tracing?
opts: Short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke

Correct. A short PR interval with a slurred upstroke of the QRS (the delta wave) in sinus rhythm is pre-excitation, consistent with an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
Long PR with every P wave conducted
A PR interval over 0.20 seconds with every P wave conducted is first-degree atrioventricular block; on this tracing the P wave runs almost straight into the QRS, so the PR is short.
Progressively longer PR, then a dropped beat
PR lengthening until a QRS drops is Mobitz type I block; here every P wave is followed by a QRS, and the striking feature is the slurred start of each QRS.
Irregular rhythm with no P waves
No P waves and an irregular rhythm describe atrial fibrillation; this tracing is in sinus rhythm, with a P wave before every QRS.
ruled out by a stated finding
set1.alt: Close-up rhythm strip of three beats, each with a small P wave running into a QRS whose upstroke is gradual before the main spike

set1.q: A 29-year-old woman has had a resting heart rate of 110 to 120 for months, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Thyroid tests, blood count, oxygen saturation and a drug screen are normal, and she takes no medications or stimulants. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A sinus tachycardia that stays unexplained after secondary causes have been excluded is inappropriate sinus tachycardia, a diagnosis of exclusion with a usually benign prognosis.
Appropriate sinus tachycardia is a response to physiologic stress, illness or a drug; every such cause has been looked for and excluded here.
ruled out by a stated finding
Focal atrial tachycardia has one abnormally shaped P wave from an ectopic focus and typically starts abruptly; her P waves are normal sinus P waves.
Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves outnumbering the QRS complexes, at an atrial rate of 250 or more; she has one normal P wave per beat.

set1.q: An 84-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has fatigue and dizziness. Her electrocardiogram shows P waves and wide QRS complexes at two separate rates with no relationship, the ventricular rate 36. She has had no tick bites, infections or recent procedures. Which cause of this rhythm is most likely?
opts: Bacterial endocarditis with an associated abscess is a listed cause of complete block, but she has had no infection; degenerative disease of old age is far more common.
ruled out by a stated finding
Lyme carditis is a listed cause of complete block, but she has had no tick bites; the most common cause in an elderly hypertensive patient is degenerative conduction disease.
ruled out by a stated finding
Increased vagal tone is a listed cause of first-degree and Mobitz type I block in conditioned people; complete block in an 84-year-old is most often degenerative.

Correct. Third-degree block is most commonly from acquired disease of the conduction system, especially degenerative changes of old age, chronic hypertension and diabetes; an elderly hypertensive patient without infection fits best.

set1.q: A 19-year-old woman has had three episodes of a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 230 that converted with adenosine. Her tracing in sinus rhythm shows a short PR interval and a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave). Which is the first-line long-term treatment?
opts: A pill-in-the-pocket beta blocker or calcium channel blocker is an option for nodal reentrant tachycardia; Wolff-Parkinson-White is treated by ablating the pathway.
Correct. A short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) marks Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, and catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line long-term treatment.
Oral beta blockers or calcium channel blockers are the initial long-term therapy for focal atrial tachycardia; for Wolff-Parkinson-White, ablation of the pathway is first line.
A permanent pacemaker treats symptomatic bradycardia and high-grade block; an accessory pathway is cured by catheter ablation.

set1.q: A 26-year-old woman with asthma used her inhaler repeatedly during an attack and then felt a sudden, rapid pounding in her chest. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves. Which factor most likely triggered this rhythm?
opts: Correct. A sudden, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with hidden P waves in a young woman is nodal reentrant tachycardia, which may start spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists or sympathomimetics.
Increased vagal tone slows conduction and appears among the causes of junctional rhythm and first-degree block, not of a sudden fast rhythm.
Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome; it slows the heart rather than triggering a reentrant tachycardia.
Low potassium is a listed cause of premature ventricular contractions and of acquired long QT; this narrow, regular tachycardia with hidden P waves is nodal reentry.

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman on several medications has recurrent palpitations and near-fainting. Monitoring shows runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose QRS complexes twist around the baseline (torsades de pointes), and her QT interval is prolonged. Which laboratory abnormality would most likely contribute?
opts: Anemia is a listed cause of sinus tachycardia, a regular narrow rhythm; acquired long QT and torsades come from drugs, low potassium and low calcium.
Correct. Most torsades de pointes comes from acquired long QT syndrome, whose causes include drugs that prolong the QT, low potassium (hypokalemia) and low calcium (hypocalcemia).
The electrolyte causes of acquired long QT on the list are low potassium and low calcium; a high potassium is not among them.
High calcium appears among the causes of premature ventricular contractions, but acquired long QT and torsades come with low calcium, along with low potassium.

set1.q: A 38-year-old man who drinks several energy drinks a day is told his skipped beats are premature ventricular contractions. Which description best fits these beats?
opts: Early and narrow, with an inverted P wave
An early narrow beat with an inverted P wave in II, III and aVF is a premature junctional contraction; a ventricular beat is wide and bizarre.
Wide, with a slurred upstroke and short PR
A short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) on every beat is pre-excitation; a premature ventricular beat is early with no P wave at all.
Early, wide and bizarre, with no P wave
Correct. A premature ventricular contraction begins in the ventricles, so the early beat has a wide (over 0.12 seconds), bizarre QRS and no P wave; caffeine and stimulants are among the triggers.
Early and narrow, with an abnormal P wave
An early narrow beat with an abnormally shaped P wave is a premature atrial contraction; a ventricular beat is wide with no P wave.

set1.q: A 62-year-old man collapses in a hospital hallway. He is unresponsive with no pulse, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation is started. His monitor strip is shown. Which is the most important next step?
opts: Amiodarone is added for ventricular fibrillation that persists after shocks and epinephrine; the first priority in this arrest is an immediate unsynchronized shock.
Transcutaneous pacing is the emergent treatment for unstable bradycardia from high-grade block; this pulseless chaotic rhythm needs defibrillation.

Correct. Chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no organized QRS complexes and no pulse is ventricular fibrillation, treated as cardiac arrest with defibrillation (an unsynchronized shock) as soon as possible, then 2 minutes of compressions.
Synchronized cardioversion times the shock to a QRS complex, so it is for a tachycardia with a pulse; ventricular fibrillation has no QRS to time to and needs defibrillation.
set1.alt: Rhythm strip of continuous, irregular, low-to-medium waves with no recognizable P waves or complexes

set1.q: A 76-year-old woman is brought in after fainting twice today. She is pale, with a blood pressure of 84/50, and her lead II rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate emergent treatment?
opts: Adenosine is used to slow or stop a regular supraventricular tachycardia, a fast rhythm; this slow rhythm with dropped QRS complexes needs pacing.
Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia with a pulse; this is a slow rhythm with dropped QRS complexes, which needs pacing.

Correct. P waves at a steady rate with a constant PR, then a P wave with no QRS, is Mobitz type II block; with fainting and hypotension the emergent treatment is transcutaneous pacing, followed by a permanent pacemaker.
A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II block, but with fainting and hypotension right now she first needs emergent transcutaneous pacing.
set1.alt: Lead II rhythm strip with regular small P waves and narrow complexes; at one point a P wave appears with no complex after it, leaving a long gap

set1.q: A 47-year-old woman 5 days after hip surgery has sudden dyspnea, chest pain and a heart rate of 118. Her new electrocardiogram shows a QRS of 0.14 seconds with an rsR' pattern (a second upward deflection) in V1 to V3. Which underlying problem best explains the new conduction finding?
opts: Lyme carditis is a listed cause of atrioventricular block, such as first-degree, Mobitz and complete block; a sudden right bundle branch block after surgery fits pulmonary embolism.
An accessory pathway produces a short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave), not an rsR' pattern; her new right bundle branch block fits pulmonary embolism.

Correct. A wide QRS with an rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 is right bundle branch block, and a sudden increase in right ventricular pressure from pulmonary embolism is a listed cause, the one that fits a sudden new block in this setting.
Valvular heart disease, especially aortic stenosis, is a listed cause of left bundle branch block; her rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 is a right bundle branch block.

opts: A premature junctional contraction is early and narrow but has an inverted P wave, a hidden P wave or a P wave after the QRS, not an abnormal upright P before it.
A premature ventricular contraction is early, wide and bizarre with no P wave in front; this early beat is narrow and has its own P wave.
ruled out by a stated finding
Mobitz type I lengthens the PR until a QRS drops, so it produces a missing beat, not an early beat with an abnormal P wave.
Correct. An early beat with its own abnormally shaped P wave and a narrow QRS is a premature atrial contraction, which can occur in normal hearts with stress, caffeine or excess alcohol.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man recovering from cardiac surgery is told his slow rhythm is a junctional rhythm. Which description best fits his tracing?
opts: Irregular and narrow, with no visible P waves
An irregular narrow rhythm without P waves is atrial fibrillation; a junctional rhythm is regular, and its P waves are inverted, buried or after the QRS.
Regular and narrow, with an upright P before each QRS
An upright P wave before each narrow QRS at a slow rate is sinus bradycardia; junctional P waves are inverted in II, III and aVF or hidden.
Regular and narrow, with inverted or hidden P waves

Correct. A junctional rhythm is regular, usually 40 to 60, with a narrow QRS; its P waves are inverted in II, III and aVF before the QRS, buried in it or after it, and recent cardiac surgery is one cause.
Regular and wide, with P waves unrelated to the QRS
P waves unrelated to a slow, often wide QRS rhythm describe third-degree block, complete dissociation of atria and ventricles; a junctional rhythm is narrow.

set2.q: A 77-year-old woman is found unresponsive and pulseless, and chest compressions are started. Her monitor strip is shown, and the same flat tracing appears in every lead. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Defibrillation treats ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia; asystole and pulseless electrical activity are unshockable.
Synchronized cardioversion needs a QRS complex to time the shock to and a patient with a pulse; asystole has neither and is unshockable.
Amiodarone is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia that persists after shocks; asystole is treated with compressions and epinephrine.

Correct. A flat line with no P waves or QRS complexes is asystole, which is unshockable: continue high-quality chest compressions and give epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes, the mainstays of treatment; the prognosis is poor.
set2.alt: Rhythm strip with a nearly flat line across the whole page and no complexes

set2.q: A 58-year-old man who takes a beta blocker has an irregular pulse at a routine visit. He has no symptoms, and his rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: First-degree block is a long but constant PR with every P wave conducted; this strip has a P wave that is not followed by a QRS.
ruled out by a stated finding
Third-degree block shows no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes; here the conducted beats keep a PR interval that lengthens in a repeating pattern.

Correct. The PR interval grows longer beat by beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, then the cycle restarts: second-degree Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block, which medications such as beta blockers can cause.
Mobitz type II keeps a constant PR interval before randomly dropped QRS complexes; on this strip the PR lengthens progressively before each drop.
set2.alt: Rhythm strip with small upright P waves and narrow complexes in groups, with a gap where one P wave stands alone

set2.q: An 80-year-old woman with heart failure and atrial fibrillation has nausea and fatigue. Her electrocardiogram now shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 46 with no visible P waves. Which of her medications best explains this rhythm?
opts: Anticholinergic drugs are a listed cause of sinus tachycardia, a fast rhythm with a P wave before each beat; her rhythm is slow with no P waves.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 40 to 60 with no visible P waves is a junctional rhythm, and digoxin toxicity is one of its listed causes, along with sinus node dysfunction, inferior infarction and recent cardiac surgery.
Apixaban is a direct oral anticoagulant preferred for stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation; it is not a listed cause of a slow junctional rhythm.
Beta-agonists and sympathomimetics are triggers of fast rhythms such as nodal reentrant tachycardia; they do not produce a slow junctional rhythm.

set2.q: A 64-year-old woman with heart failure has had a regular, wide-complex tachycardia at 150 for 40 minutes, every QRS the same shape. She is alert, with no chest pain or shortness of breath and a blood pressure of 126/78. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic tachycardia of a long QT; her complexes are all one shape, so this is monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.

Correct. Regular wide complexes of one shape for over 30 seconds are sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, often seen with heart failure; she is hemodynamically stable, so the treatment is pharmacologic cardioversion with an intravenous antiarrhythmic such as amiodarone.

Defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion) is for pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation; she is alert with a pulse and a normal blood pressure, so she gets pharmacologic cardioversion.

Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse (chest pain, confusion, dyspnea, hypotension); she has none of these, so she gets pharmacologic cardioversion.

opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular too, but it has a P wave before every QRS in at least three shapes; he has no P waves.
ruled out by a stated finding
Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves and is usually regular because the node blocks a fixed share of them; his rhythm has no atrial waves and no pattern.
Sinus arrhythmia keeps a P wave before every beat and varies with breathing at 60 to 100; he has no P waves and a rate of 130.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. An irregularly irregular, narrow-complex rhythm with absent P waves and no PR interval is atrial fibrillation; obesity, sleep apnea and older age are among its common associations.

set2.q: A 69-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes has newly found atrial fibrillation, now rate controlled. Her HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score is 1, low risk. Which tool now decides whether she needs anticoagulation?
opts: QRS width separates narrow supraventricular from wide ventricular rhythms; the anticoagulation decision in atrial fibrillation rests on the stroke-risk score.

Correct. With her bleeding risk low, the decision rests on stroke risk, assessed with the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score: 0 in men or 1 in women is low risk and may not require anticoagulation, while most others need it.
Anticoagulation is withheld when bleeding risk is high, but her HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score is 1, low risk, so anticoagulation is okay; whether she needs it is set by the stroke-risk score.
The heart rate guides rate control, the first goal of treatment; the anticoagulation decision rests on the stroke-risk score, with low risk 0 for men or 1 for women.

set2.q: A 68-year-old woman admitted with pneumonia has new, frequent early, wide, bizarre beats without P waves on the monitor. Which is the most important initial evaluation?
opts: Correct. Premature ventricular contractions are mainly caused by hypoxemia or electrolyte imbalance (low potassium, low magnesium, high calcium), so oxygenation and electrolytes are checked first.
Urgent angiography follows defibrillation of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; new premature ventricular contractions in a sick inpatient call first for oxygen and electrolytes.
Ambulatory monitoring checks whether symptoms match intermittent bradycardia; her early beats are already on the monitor, and their usual causes are hypoxemia and electrolytes.
The stroke-risk score guides anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation; premature ventricular contractions carry no such decision and call for oxygen and electrolytes.

opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia has one P wave per QRS in at least three shapes; here several identical sawtooth waves fall between each pair of QRS complexes.
Sinus tachycardia has one upright P wave before each QRS at 100 to 160; this strip has several identical atrial waves for every QRS, the sawtooth of flutter.

Correct. Repeating sawtooth (flutter) waves outnumber the narrow QRS complexes because the atrioventricular node blocks some of them: atrial flutter, common after atrial scarring from cardiac surgery.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no organized atrial waves; this strip shows regular, repeating sawtooth waves between the QRS complexes.

opts: A premature atrial contraction has an early, abnormally shaped P wave from the atria, but an inverted P in II, III and aVF with a short PR marks a junctional origin.
A premature ventricular contraction is early, wide and bizarre with no P wave; this early beat is narrow and carries an inverted P wave.
ruled out by a stated finding
Wolff-Parkinson-White gives a short PR on every sinus beat, with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave); here only the occasional early beat differs.
Correct. An early, narrow QRS whose P wave is inverted in II, III and aVF with a short PR comes from the atrioventricular junction: a premature junctional contraction, usually without symptoms.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted in respiratory distress. His pulse is fast and irregular, and his rhythm strip is shown, with arrows marking P waves. Which description best fits this tracing?
opts: Regular, with sawtooth waves between beats
Regular sawtooth waves outnumbering the QRS complexes are atrial flutter; this strip shows separate P waves of varying shape, one before each QRS, at irregular intervals.
Irregular, with several different P-wave shapes

Correct. An irregular, narrow-complex tachycardia with a P wave before each QRS in at least three different shapes in the same lead is multifocal atrial tachycardia, typical of acutely ill patients with severe lung disease.
Irregularly irregular, with no visible P waves
No P waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm describe atrial fibrillation; on this strip the arrows point to P waves, and their shape changes from beat to beat.
Regular, with one abnormal P-wave shape
A regular rhythm with one consistently abnormal P wave is focal atrial tachycardia from a single ectopic focus; this rhythm is irregular, with P waves of changing shape.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman has a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 210 with no visible P waves. She is confused and pale, with a blood pressure of 70/40. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A vagal maneuver is first line only for stable supraventricular tachycardia; hemodynamic instability calls for immediate synchronized cardioversion.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with hidden P waves is supraventricular tachycardia; confusion and hypotension make it hemodynamically unstable, which calls for immediate synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock with decreased voltage.
Defibrillation (an unsynchronized shock) is for pulseless ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation; she has an organized rhythm, so the shock is synchronized.
Adenosine follows a vagal maneuver in stable supraventricular tachycardia; she is confused and hypotensive, which calls for an immediate synchronized shock.

set2.q: A 63-year-old man started a new medication 2 weeks ago and now feels tired. His electrocardiogram shows a regular rate of 48 with an upright P wave before every narrow QRS and a PR interval of 0.18 seconds. Which medication class most likely explains this rhythm?
opts: Beta-agonists and other sympathomimetics trigger fast rhythms such as nodal reentrant tachycardia; they do not slow the sinus node to 48.

Correct. A regular rhythm under 60 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus bradycardia; beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin are its listed drug causes.
Anticholinergic drugs are listed causes of sinus tachycardia, which speeds the sinus rate; his sinus rhythm is slow, at 48.
Stimulants speed the heart and are listed causes of sinus tachycardia; a slow sinus rhythm points instead to a beta blocker, calcium channel blocker or digoxin.

set2.q: A 34-year-old man was bitten by a tick while hiking a month ago and now feels lightheaded. He takes no medications. His electrocardiogram shows the PR interval growing longer with each beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, and then the cycle repeats. Which underlying cause is most likely?
opts: Correct. Progressive PR lengthening ending in a dropped QRS is Mobitz type I block, and Lyme disease (Lyme carditis), after a tick bite, is one of its listed causes along with vagal tone, medications, ischemia and ablation.
Degenerative changes of old age drive first-degree, Mobitz type II and complete block; in a 34-year-old with a recent tick bite, Lyme carditis fits best.
ruled out by a stated finding
Digoxin is a listed medication cause of Mobitz type I block, but he takes no medications; the recent tick bite points to Lyme carditis.
ruled out by a stated finding
Increased vagal tone is a listed cause of Mobitz type I, but nothing in his history suggests it; the recent tick bite points to Lyme carditis.

opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with at least three P-wave shapes, usually in acutely ill lung patients; her rhythm is regular with no visible P waves.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular; her tachycardia is regular, starts suddenly and comes with neck pulsations, which fits nodal reentry.

Correct. A sudden, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with hidden P waves and neck pulsations (frog sign) in a young woman is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, a reentry circuit within the node, far more common in women.
Focal atrial tachycardia shows one abnormal P wave before every QRS; her P waves are hidden, and the neck pulsations of the frog sign point to nodal reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction wears a 24-hour monitor. It shows several runs of 5 to 8 consecutive wide, identical beats at 150, each lasting under 10 seconds and stopping on its own. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sustained ventricular tachycardia lasts 30 seconds or more or causes collapse sooner; his runs end on their own in under 10 seconds.
Premature atrial contractions are single early narrow beats with abnormal P waves; his runs are wide, consecutive and ventricular.
Ventricular fibrillation is uncoordinated activity with no pulse and no perfusion; his runs are organized, identical wide beats that stop on their own.

Correct. Three or more consecutive premature ventricular beats is ventricular tachycardia, and runs lasting under 30 seconds are nonsustained; identical QRS shapes make it monomorphic, which is common with heart disease such as prior infarction.

set2.q: A 57-year-old woman whose QT interval became prolonged after starting a new medication has palpitations, and the monitor shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose QRS complexes twist around the baseline (torsades de pointes). She is awake, and intravenous magnesium has been given. If an antiarrhythmic is added, which one can be used?
opts: Correct. In torsades de pointes magnesium is the treatment, and intravenous lidocaine is the antiarrhythmic that can be used (with little evidence), because amiodarone and procainamide prolong the QT and beta blockers lengthen it indirectly.
Amiodarone is avoided in torsades de pointes because it prolongs the QT further; lidocaine is the antiarrhythmic that can be used.
Procainamide is avoided in torsades de pointes because it prolongs the QT; it is used instead for pre-excited atrial fibrillation and stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.
Beta blockers such as metoprolol are avoided in torsades de pointes because the bradycardia they cause lengthens the R-to-R interval and indirectly the QT.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy and a reduced ejection fraction has worsening dyspnea and fatigue despite medical therapy. His electrocardiogram shows a QRS of 0.16 seconds with a dominant S wave in V1 and monophasic R waves in I, V5 and V6. Which is the most appropriate treatment for this conduction problem?
opts: Most left bundle branch block is left untreated, but symptomatic block with reduced ejection fraction is the exception that gets a biventricular pacemaker.
Catheter ablation treats accessory pathways, focal atrial tachycardia and some ventricular rhythms; a symptomatic left bundle branch block with low ejection fraction gets biventricular pacing.
Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia; left bundle branch block is a conduction delay in sinus rhythm, treated here with a biventricular pacemaker.

Correct. A wide QRS with a dominant S wave in V1 and monophasic lateral R waves is left bundle branch block; it is usually left untreated, except symptomatic block with reduced ejection fraction, which gets a biventricular pacemaker.

opts: Lidocaine is a choice for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, which is regular at about 150 to 200; this wide rhythm is irregular and approaches 300.

Correct. A very fast, irregular rhythm with wide complexes of changing width is atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway (pre-excited atrial fibrillation); intravenous procainamide is used, never adenosine.
When atrial fibrillation runs with Wolff-Parkinson-White, adenosine must not be used; the drug for pre-excited atrial fibrillation is intravenous procainamide.
Intravenous rate control suits ordinary atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate; an irregular, wide rhythm through an accessory pathway is treated with procainamide.

set2.q: A 77-year-old woman has no symptoms, but her routine electrocardiogram shows P waves at a steady rate with a constant PR interval and an occasional P wave not followed by a QRS. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Correct. A constant PR with randomly dropped QRS complexes is Mobitz type II block, dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression to complete block and sudden death; the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Observation suits asymptomatic first-degree or Mobitz type I block; Mobitz type II is dangerous even without symptoms and needs a permanent pacemaker.
Beta blockers are listed causes of first-degree and Mobitz type I block, not a treatment for block; Mobitz type II needs a permanent pacemaker.
Catheter ablation is itself a listed cause of Mobitz type II block and treats accessory pathways or reentry; this block needs a permanent pacemaker.

set2.q: A 79-year-old woman has spells of a racing heartbeat followed by near-fainting. Her ambulatory monitor strip is shown, and her near-fainting spells match the long pauses. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Observation is appropriate in sick sinus syndrome only when symptoms fail to correlate with the bradycardia; her near-fainting matches the pauses, so she needs a pacemaker.
ruled out by a stated finding
Atropine is the first-line drug for acute, unstable sinus bradycardia; chronic, recurrent symptomatic pauses from a sick sinus node are treated with a permanent pacemaker.
Adenosine is used for stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver; it does nothing for the pauses that are causing her near-fainting spells.

Correct. Bursts of a rapid rhythm that stop into long pauses before slow beats return are tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sick sinus syndrome; when symptoms correlate with the bradycardia, a permanent pacemaker is the treatment.

set2.q: An 81-year-old man reports dizziness and two fainting spells. His pulse is 36, and his rhythm strip is shown, with arrows marking R waves and P waves. Which description best fits this tracing?
opts: PR lengthens until a QRS is dropped
Progressive PR lengthening before a dropped QRS is Mobitz type I block; here the P waves keep no consistent relation to the QRS at all.
Constant PR with an occasional dropped QRS
A constant PR with occasional dropped beats is Mobitz type II block; on this strip the distance from P wave to QRS changes every beat.
Every P wave conducted with a long PR
A long, constant PR with every P wave conducted is first-degree block; here most P waves are not followed by a QRS, and the two run at different rates.
P waves and QRS complexes at unrelated rates

Correct. The P waves march at their own regular rate and the slow QRS complexes at another, with no fixed relation: complete dissociation of the atria from the ventricles, third-degree (complete) block, ventricular rate usually under 40.

set2.q: A 59-year-old woman with crushing chest pain becomes lightheaded but stays awake, with a pulse and a blood pressure of 104/66. Her QT interval was normal on a tracing an hour ago, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is used for unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse; polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated.
Amiodarone may be added after the shock, but drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia; polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable.
Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, the polymorphic tachycardia of a prolonged QT; her QT was normal, which points to ischemia and calls for defibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Wide complexes that keep changing shape are polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; even when the patient looks well it is never truly stable, a short-lived transitional state that needs defibrillation.

set2.q: An 80-year-old man is brought in dizzy and confused, with a blood pressure of 78/44. His electrocardiogram shows P waves at 76 and wide QRS complexes at 32, with no relationship between them. Which is the most appropriate emergent treatment?
opts: Correct. Atria and ventricles beating at separate rates is third-degree (complete) block; with confusion and hypotension the emergent treatment is transcutaneous pacing, and the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for complete block, but a confused, hypotensive patient needs emergent transcutaneous pacing first.
Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia; this is a slow escape rhythm at 32 from complete block, which needs pacing.
Amiodarone treats ventricular tachycardia, a fast wide rhythm; a slow escape rhythm at 32 from complete block needs transcutaneous pacing.

set2.q: A 74-year-old man with diabetes is told his new palpitations come from atrial fibrillation. Which description best fits his electrocardiogram?
opts: Irregularly irregular, with no P waves
Correct. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no PR interval; the QRS is narrow, and the rate is often 110 to 160 but can be under 80 or over 200.
Regular, with sawtooth waves between beats
Regular sawtooth waves describe atrial flutter, in which the node conducts a fixed share of the waves; atrial fibrillation has no organized atrial activity.
Regular, with a P wave before each beat
A regular rhythm with a P wave before each beat is a sinus rhythm; atrial fibrillation has no P waves and no regularity.
Irregular, with three or more P-wave shapes
Irregular beats with three or more P-wave shapes are multifocal atrial tachycardia; atrial fibrillation has no P waves to count.

opts: Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 130 with an upright P wave before every QRS is sinus tachycardia, which usually reflects a physiologic or pathologic process; hyperthyroidism is one of the listed pathologic causes.
Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, slowing the rate below 60; this sinus rhythm is fast, which points the other way.
Digoxin is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, along with beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers; it slows the sinus rate rather than speeding it.
Increased intracranial pressure appears among the causes of sinus bradycardia, not tachycardia; a fast sinus rhythm comes from pain, anxiety, hypovolemia, anemia, hypoxia or hyperthyroidism.

opts: A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia and high-grade block; it has no role in ending a fast reentrant rhythm.

Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver and then adenosine, which may be given twice; it may convert the rhythm or at least slow it so any P waves can be seen.
Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia; he is alert with a normal blood pressure, so adenosine comes next.
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway, an irregular wide rhythm; his is regular and narrow.

opts: A junctional rhythm is regular and narrow at 40 to 60 with inverted or hidden P waves; she has regular upright P waves at 80 running separately from a wide rhythm at 34.
Sinus bradycardia has a P wave before every QRS with a normal PR; her atrial rate is 80 while the ventricles beat at 34, unrelated.

opts: Ambulatory monitoring catches intermittent rhythms and checks symptom correlation; this sustained tachycardia is happening now and is captured with a 12-lead tracing.
The stroke-risk score decides anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation; stable sustained ventricular tachycardia calls first for a 12-lead tracing and labs.

Correct. Stable sustained ventricular tachycardia is managed first with a cardiac monitor, intravenous access, supplemental oxygen, appropriate labs and a 12-lead electrocardiogram, before pharmacologic cardioversion.
